title: The trial
hookLine: he was flogged for refusing a state doctrine that the Qur'an was created

lines: A MAN IN CHAINS, ONE QUESTION.
cards: A room in the caliph's palace, and a man in chains. The question put to him is short: is the Qur'an created? Say yes, and you go home.
Judges have said yes. Other scholars, under pressure, have said yes. He won't.
He asks his questioners for a verse of the Qur'an, or a word from the Prophet, that says it. They don't give him one he accepts. So the whips come out.
The man is Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the collector from yesterday, and the ordeal has a name.

teach.b: The name is the mihnah: the trial, the ordeal. It began under the caliph al-Ma'mun.
His court had taken up a position held by theologians called the Mu'tazila: that the Qur'an, as God's speech, was created, not eternal with God.
They held it, as they understood it, to protect God's oneness: if the Qur'an is eternal alongside God, aren't there two eternal things?

Ahmad and the hadith scholars around him held the opposite: the Qur'an is the speech of God, and God's speech is not a created thing. The caliph ordered judges and scholars questioned. One after another, people gave way.
Ahmad refused. He was imprisoned, and under the next caliph, al-Mu'tasim, he was flogged.

teach.h: GIVE ME A VERSE, AND I'LL SAY IT.
teach.b: The reports keep returning to one reply: give me something from the Book of God or the sunnah of His Messenger, and I'll say it. He wasn't trying to win a philosophy debate on the court's terms.
He was refusing to make the texts say something he didn't find in them. In the end he was released, and later, under another caliph, the mihnah ended.
The Qur'an speaks of testing too: God will try people with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops, and gives good news to those who are patient.
To be fair to both sides: the Mu'tazila saw themselves defending God's unity, and Ahmad saw himself defending the text. Muslim theologians still study both arguments.
What the story keeps, especially in the Hanbali school, is one scholar who would not say it.

how: Hanbali scholars and students tell the story of Ahmad ibn Hanbal's trial as an example of steadfastness, and Sunni creeds state that the Qur'an is the uncreated speech of God.

games.q: you're Ahmad, in chains before the caliph's questioners. say the Qur'an is created and you go home. what do you say?
o: ask for a verse or a report that says it, and refuse without one.
games.why: give me something from the Book of God or the sunnah, he answers, and I'll say it. they didn't, and he wouldn't.

practice: Choose one thing you actually live by, not an opinion you'd argue online but something you keep: you don't lie to your kids, you keep the fast, you show up when you said you would.

Name it in one plain sentence, picture the pressure that might bend it, a tired evening, a boss, a friend's teasing, and say the sentence again quietly; you don't need to fight anyone, just know where you stand.
If you pray, you can ask to be kept firm.

wordCard.voice: Mihnah. Trial, ordeal: the caliph's test that demanded scholars say the Qur'an was created, and that Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: trial, ordeal; the name for the caliphs' test of scholars over whether the Qur'an was created.

carryVoice: Your line: he would not say it. Steady, and still fair to the other side. Take care tonight.
